items.name: Readability
items.evidence: No script was saved. All the work ran as inline `python3 -c` one-liners with short names like `wal`, `dec`, `dec_wal`, `cur`, and the decrypt step has no explanatory comment. It is readable but not re-runnable, which falls short of the 'small decrypt script' convention.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No reusable decrypt or extract script was left behind. Decrypt, overwrite and extract all happen in one ad-hoc inline command (step 9). The scratch experiments are kept out of /app, so there are no leftover files there, but the run can't be repeated.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The final step hardcodes `b ^ 0x42` and overwrites main.db-wal in place without first checking that the decrypted magic is 0x377f0682/3. There is no error handling, but nothing is silently swallowed.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The key comes from the header: `0x753d44c0 ^ 0x42424242 = 0x377f0682`. The whole file was decrypted and SQLite replayed the WAL. The agent checked the checkpointed pages against WAL frames, got `integrity_check: ok`, confirmed 11 rows, and compared against the 5-row no-WAL baseline.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: Copies (orig_main.db, orig_main.db-wal) were made in a scratch dir, but in the root-owned /app the WAL was rewritten in place (step 9) with no backup there, and main.db was modified. The damage is limited because the XOR is reversible, and the earlier scratch test was run on copies.
